newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh budget draws opposition fire.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh budget draws opposition fire.

text.p: An opposition leader and former finance minister said on Saturday that measures proposed in Bangladesh's 1997/98 budget would scare away investors and hurt the economy.

"The government has proposed VAT (Value Added Tax) on cottage industry. This will restrict employment and impede growth of small industries," Mohammad Saifur Rahman, leader of the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), told a news conference.
The VAT rate in Bangladesh is 15 percent.

Rahman said the new July-June budget, announced on Thursday in parliament by Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria, also levied surcharge at a rate of 2.5 percent on all imports. "This is a repressive tax which a reform-minded government cannot impose," he said.
Rahman said the present government, which came to power in June last year by defeating the BNP of former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, had altered many good moves of the past government.
He also criticised the government for "mismanagement" in the country's financial sector which resulted in dwindling foreign exchange reserves and liquidity shortfall in banks.
"The macro-economic stability is in a fragile state which may discourage foreign investment in the country," Rahman said.
He said the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina had failed to keep the economy moving as the country's export growth dropped much below the 35 percent rate achieved during "our time."
"Except for agriculture the growth in all sectors of the economy dropped (in 1996/97)," he said.

Rahman questioned the authenticity of 5.7 percent growth in the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) estimated for 1996/97, saying the growth of 5.4 percent recorded in 1995/96 was spectacular despite political unrest in the country.

Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria defended the budget at a news conference on Friday, saying the fiscal measures and development strategy would improve the lives of millions of poor people and spur economic growth.

In the new budget he proposed a 81.62 billion taka ($1.9 billion) deficit for the new fiscal yaer, starting on July 1. Revenue was envisaged at 196.24 billion taka against expenditure of 277.86 billion.
Kibria also forecast more robust growth over the next few years, predicting GDP would expand by 7.0 percent between fiscal 1997/98 and 2001/2, against an average 4.5 percent during 1991-96.

In a bid to boost business activity, Kibria proposed to cut corporate tax for banks, insurance companies and financial institutions to 40 percent from 45 percent. He also proposed reducing the highest rate of customs duty to 42.5 percent for 1997/98 from the present 45 percent.
The budget allocated 23.3 percent of its spending to alleviate poverty, with subsidies for agriculture, housing and a monthly pension allowance for 450,000 poverty-stricken elderly people.
